title: Client proto/json decoding, thread affinity, and GIL observations
content:
Summary:

This is a working note capturing a focused investigation into CPU-side latency contributions coming from client message decoding (protobuf & JSON), Python GIL behavior during handoff across our thread pool, and how thread affinity affects tail latency in the serving runtime. Goal is to identify low-effort mitigations to reduce 99th/99.9th percentile latencies for small (<1KB) requests at moderate QPS (50-200 per GPU).

Motivation / Symptoms observed:
- Several p99 latency spikes correlate with increases in CPU sys/user time on the host even when GPU queueing is low.
- Flamegraphs show long stacks in Python C extension decode/parse functions, plus long contiguous spans holding the GIL.
- Increasing request concurrency in benchmark (wrk2 + small payloads) causes tail latency to degrade supralinearly even though average CPU utilization isn't saturated.

Hypotheses:
1) Client-side protocol decode (protobuf.ParseFromString or json.loads) is single-threaded and holds the GIL for significant time per request, blocking other Python worker threads.
2) Thread pool scheduling + OS thread affinity causes hot threads to compete on same core(s), increasing preemption and context switches — this amplifies tail latency under bursts.
3) Deserialization allocates many small objects and triggers Python allocator/GC overhead contributing to latency spikes.

Benchmark environment (baseline):
- Instance: c6i.4xlarge-equivalent (16 vCPU) in k8s nodepool for serving runtime, worker processes pinned 1:1 to GPU.
- Runtime: Python 3.11.6, uvloop in front, serving runtime process spawns a fixed threadpool of 8 worker threads for request decoding + scheduling to GPU.
- Workload: synthetic client sending small prompt JSON (payload ~700 bytes), QPS: 150 steady, 10k requests total.
- Tools used: perf record + FlameGraph, py-spy top/record, strace for syscall spikes, heaptrack for allocations, python-tracemalloc, and top/htop for quick checks.

Commands run (examples):
- py-spy record -o pyspy.svg --pid <pid> --subprocesses --duration 120
- perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 120; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
- wrk2 -t4 -c200 -d120 -R150 --latency http://<endpoint>/v1/complete (with small JSON body)

Key observations:
- py-spy flamegraphs consistently show significant time in: _PyObject_Malloc -> protobuf C extension decode -> PyObject_New -> (then Python-level object building). For json inputs using json.loads(), the C parse loops are similarly long.
- The heavy stacks appear on a small subset of threads (2-3) which are pinned to the same core by the kernel. The other threads are mostly idle/waiting.
- When artificially changing threadpool size from 8 -> 16, average latency dips slightly but p99 improves only when we also change thread affinity (see experiments).
- strace shows bursts of futex and epoll_wait around the same time as the latency spikes -> suggests lock contention around Python runtime or internal threadpool handoff.
- tracemalloc sampling shows many short-lived small allocations from the decoder path; peaks in allocations align with p99 spikes.

Micro-experiments and results:
1) Move decoding to a dedicated process (multiprocess worker) using multiprocessing.Queue and msgpack between processes:
   - Result: p99 latency reduced ~30% at same QPS. CPU overhead moved to a separate process which freed main process threads quicker.
   - Tradeoffs: increases inter-process copy cost; needs careful socket buffer sizing.

2) Swap json.loads -> orjson.loads for JSON paths:
   - Result: median slightly reduced, p99 improved ~12–18%. CPU profile shows less time in C-level JSON parser.

3) Replace Python protobuf C-extension decode with custom Cython wrapper that decodes into preallocated buffers (experimental):
   - Result: non-trivial engineering effort. Early prototype reduced allocations but still held GIL during decode. p99 improves modestly.

4) Thread affinity tweaks: pin threads round-robin across cores instead of default kernel scheduling; set CPU sets for worker threads (sched_setaffinity)
   - Result: tail latency improved up to ~25% in some runs because scheduler-related preemption dropped. However, over-pin can cause load imbalance; best results when pooling affinity across 2 cores per hot thread.

5) Experiment with subinterpreters (PEP 554-style ideas):
   - Not production-ready. Subinterpreters reduce GIL interference only if C-extension respects subinterpreter reentrancy; protobuf C ext does not, so limited benefit.

Profiling snippets (representative call stacks observed):
- _PyObject_Malloc -> PyUnicode_New -> PyBytes_FromStringAndSize -> google::protobuf::internal::ParseField
- PyEval_EvalFrameEx (holding GIL) -> request_handler -> decode_client_message -> protobuf.ParseFromString

Interim conclusions / root causes:
- Deserialization is indeed a dominant contributor to CPU tail latency; the C-extension parsing holds the GIL long enough to block other Python threads in our worker pool.
- Thread scheduling and affinity issues exacerbate the problem; when several threads holding the GIL are pinned to same core, preemption and context switches blow up tail latencies.
- Memory allocations from the decoder are frequent and increase GC pressure; short-lived object churn increases overhead under bursty loads.

Practical mitigations (prioritized):
1) Move blocking/deserializing work out of the shared Python threadpool into an isolated pool of processes (worker subprocesses). This yielded biggest win with minimal changes.
2) Replace slow Python-level parsing with faster libraries where safe: orjson for JSON; for protobuf, evaluate nanopb or streaming parse options to reduce allocations.
3) Use explicit thread affinity/CPU set tuning in the k8s pod to avoid hot-thread collisions. Automate via startup script that pins worker threads in round-robin fashion across free cores.
4) Reuse buffers (bytearray/memoryview) for decode targets to cut allocator churn; add a small object pool for frequently allocated structures.
5) Audit C extension decode paths for GIL release opportunities. If feasible, upstream or patch the pb ext to release GIL around heavy CPU loops.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we get a quantifiable cost/benefit of moving to subprocess decode for production traffic patterns (not just synthetic)? Need end-to-end A/B.
- Are there ABI-compatible protobuf alternatives that release GIL during parse? We should evaluate protobuf-c, nanopb, and rapidjson for structured payloads.
- How does network stack (kernel) interplay with CPU contention? Need to correlate tcp_rx queueing with decode spikes.
- Would adding an asio-like dedicated decode thread in native code (C++) be best long term to avoid Python GIL entirely for parsing?

Next steps (short term):
- Implement a production-ready subprocess decode worker with a bounded queue (+ backpressure) and test for 1 week on staging using real traffic replay. Owner: Marco. Priority: high.
- Experiment orjson for all JSON endpoints behind a feature flag. Owner: Evelyn. Priority: medium.
- Add a pod-level startup script to set cpuset/thread affinity for hot threads and measure improvement. Owner: Samir. Priority: medium.
- Open a PR to add tracelogging for allocation spikes during decode paths to correlate with p99 spikes. Owner: Asha. Priority: low/medium.

Notes to self (TODOs / rough):
- Capture perf map + py-spy from a real customer replay (need approval).
- Try constructing a microbenchmark that only exercises protobuf decode to get deterministic numbers (single-threaded vs multi-threaded).
- Check kernel sched_debug logs around a tail spike timestamp to see if throttling or load balancing events show up.

References and artifacts:
- perf.svg, pyspy.svg, perf_out.folded (links in linked_artifacts above + internal S3).
- Related older notes: request-parse-epoll-flamegraph-audit.json (see shared drive).

If you read this and have ideas: ping me in #eng-serving-runtime; I think there are quick wins that can be shipped in a week but some fixes (C extension/GIL release) require deeper work and coordination with protobuf maintainers.

-- Asha
